summary.heading: Wavefronts, rays and reflection
summary.html:
• A wavefront joins neighbouring points in phase (for example along a crest); neighbouring wavefronts are one wavelength apart.
  • A ray shows the direction of travel of the wave and its energy, always perpendicular to the wavefronts.
  • At a boundary, part of a wave is usually reflected and part transmitted.
  • All angles are measured from the normal. Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection. On reflection, speed, frequency and wavelength are unchanged.

summary.heading: Refraction, Snell's law and total internal reflection
summary.html:
• Refraction: a change of direction at a boundary because the speed changes. The frequency is fixed, so the wavelength changes in proportion to the speed.
  • Slowing down: bends towards the normal. Speeding up: bends away. Along the normal: no change of direction, but speed and wavelength still change.
  • Refractive index $n = \dfrac{c}{v}$ (air 1.00, water 1.33, glass about 1.5).
$$\frac{n_1}{n_2} = \frac{\sin\theta_2}{\sin\theta_1} = \frac{v_2}{v_1}$$
  • Equivalently $n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$, where medium 1 is the one the wave comes from.
  • Critical angle: going into a medium with a lower refractive index, the refracted ray runs along the boundary when $\sin\theta_c = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$ ($n_1 > n_2$).
  • Beyond $\theta_c$, all the light is reflected: total internal reflection. Uses: optical fibres (with a lower-index cladding), endoscopes, the sparkle of diamonds.

summary.heading: Diffraction
summary.html:
• Diffraction is the spreading of a wave through a gap or around an obstacle. Wavelength, frequency and speed are unchanged; only the wavefront shape changes.
  • Most noticeable when the gap or obstacle is similar in size to the wavelength; a much wider gap gives little spreading.
  • So sound (wavelength about 1 m) diffracts round doorways but light (about $5 \times 10^{-7}$ m) doesn't, and long-wavelength radio reaches valleys behind hills.
  • Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront is a source of new wavelets; a narrow gap acts like a point source.

summary.heading: Superposition and interference
summary.html:
• Principle of superposition: where waves overlap, the total displacement is the sum of the individual displacements (with signs). Afterwards, each wave carries on unchanged.
  • Crest meets crest: constructive; crest meets an equal trough: destructive.
  • A steady interference pattern needs coherent sources: the same frequency and a constant phase difference. For light, both sources come from one source (a laser through two slits).
$$\text{constructive: path difference} = n\lambda$$ $$\text{destructive: path difference} = \left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$$
  • (For sources in phase, $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$)
  • Young's double slit: equally spaced bright and dark fringes on a distant screen.
$$s = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$$
  • $s$ = fringe separation, $d$ = slit separation, $D$ = slits-to-screen distance. Fringes spread out for longer $\lambda$, larger $D$ or smaller $d$.
  • Measure across several fringes and divide, to reduce the percentage uncertainty in $s$.

summary.heading: Single-slit diffraction and the double-slit envelope
summary.html:
• A single slit of width $b$ gives a wide, bright central maximum, twice as wide as each much dimmer side maximum.
$$\theta = \frac{\lambda}{b}$$
  • $\theta$ is the angle to the first minimum, in radians (small angles). Distance on the screen $\approx D\theta$; the central maximum is $2D\theta$ wide.
  • A narrower slit or longer wavelength gives a wider pattern; a narrower slit also makes it dimmer.
  • White light: white centre with coloured edges (blue inside, red outside).
  • In a double-slit experiment, each slit's single-slit pattern modulates the fringes: they stay equally spaced but their brightness follows the single-slit envelope, and a fringe that falls on a single-slit minimum is missing.

summary.heading: Multiple slits and diffraction gratings
summary.html:
• More slits with the same spacing: maxima in the same positions as for two slits, but narrower and brighter, with faint secondary maxima between.
$$n\lambda = d\sin\theta$$
  • $n$ = order (0 straight through), $d$ = line spacing; $N$ lines per metre gives $d = 1/N$. No small-angle approximation.
  • Highest order: the largest whole number $n$ less than $d/\lambda$ (since $\sin\theta$ must be less than 1).
  • White light: white central maximum; each other order is a spectrum, violet nearest the centre, red furthest. Higher orders can overlap.
  • Sharp maxima make gratings ideal for measuring wavelengths precisely (spectrometers, E.1).

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal.
  • Saying the frequency changes on refraction.
  • Saying total internal reflection can happen going into a higher-index medium.
  • Saying diffraction changes the wavelength.
  • Forgetting the coherence condition.
  • Mixing up $d$ and $D$, or not converting mm and nm to m.
  • HL Using degrees in $\theta = \lambda/b$.
  • HL Swapping slit width $b$ and spacing $d$ between the two formulas, or giving an order where $\sin\theta > 1$.

Competing theories: Both theories explained reflection and refraction. Which observation could tell them apart? (Hint: what does each predict for the speed of light in water?)
How much should a scientist's reputation count when judging a theory? Can students think of a modern example?
Evidence: Young's fringes were not accepted straight away. Why might strong evidence take years to change a community's mind?
Students do the double-slit experiment with a laser. What exactly in the pattern counts as evidence for waves rather than particles?
Falsification: Poisson made a prediction he expected to fail. Why is a risky prediction that comes true more convincing than a safe one?
If Arago had not seen the spot, would the wave theory have been finished? What else might scientists have blamed?

oracy.html:
Think–pair–share (1 minute alone, 3 minutes in pairs, then pairs report to the class). Question: "From the bank you see a fish lying still under a calm pond. To light it up with a laser pointer, should you aim straight at where you see it, below it, or above it?"

  • We think … because …
  • A ray diagram shows …
  • The strongest objection to our view is …

Listen for: aim straight at it; light paths are reversible, so the beam refracts at the surface and follows the same path back to the fish.

How does a community choose between theo: Ask students to list factors other than evidence that influenced the light debate (reputation, nationality, mathematical tools). Should any of them matter?
Is there a point where a theory has been tested enough to call it true?
Can trying to disprove a theory prove it: Popper argued theories can be falsified but never proved. Does the Poisson spot prove the wave theory, or only fail to disprove it?
Light later turned out to have particle properties too (E.2). Was the Arago experiment misleading?
How simple is too simple?: Young's formula ignores slit width, yet it gives good wavelengths. When does a missing detail start to matter?
Compare this with leaving out air resistance in A.1. Is there a general rule for what can be left out?
Can something be two things at once?: Is "wave" a description of what light is, or of how it behaves in certain experiments?
Can students think of other things described by two different models depending on the question asked?
